problems.field: participants.n_analyzed and participants.counts_are (also participants.who, participants.population, arms[Human dyads].n_analyzed)
problems.form_value: n_analyzed 20 with counts_are 'teams'; who: '20 human dyads. This paper does not describe who they were or give the number of people.'; population 'not_stated'; Human dyads arm n_analyzed 20
problems.source_says: The S2 count is 20 pairs of people, not people. The paper defines a dyad as a team of two humans, so the 20 pre-study dyads are 40 people, and the codebook counts people. The pre-study itself (reference [7], candidate c151, read at the URL that c032 prints) states 40 participants: students at an Austrian university, mostly psychology students, from the face-to-face group (20 dyads) of an Oct-Nov 2023 study on face-to-face vs video-conference collaboration. S2 is unrandomized context, so eligibility is unaffected.
problems.quote: we compared human dyads (= teams of two humans) ... compared to 20 human dyads. [7]: The 40 human participants were students from an Austrian university (mostly psychology students)
problems.locator: c032 p. 4, Section 3 (dyad definition; also p. 1, Section 1) and Section 4.1; [7] Bangerl, Stefan, Pammer-Schindler (2024), TREW 2024 workshop paper, p. 3, Sections 4.2-4.3

problems.form_value: The Spearman correlation in Figure 14 (rho_s = 0.424, p = 0.002) is labeled dyads, nAI = 26.
problems.source_says: The label is quoted correctly, but the printed p-value does not fit 26 dyads. With rho = 0.424, n = 26 gives t = 2.29 and p of about 0.031, while n = 52 gives t = 3.31 and p of about 0.002, as printed (my arithmetic). So this test, like the elaboration U tests, appears to use 52 participant rows with each dyad's values entered twice. The form sets the label beside the U tests as if this test were dyad-level, and the notes repeat p = 0.002 with no caveat. No participant count in the form changes.
problems.quote: a significant positive medium correlation [15] of the acceptance rate with the fluency score in the main test (ρs = 0.424, p = 0.002) | Figure 14: Fluency Score (dyads, nAI = 26)

confirmed.statement: S1 participants.n_analyzed = 104 people and arms[].n_analyzed = 52 each match the text: 'The valid sample consisted of 52 dyads/104 participants, with 26 dyads/52 participants per experimental condition.' The abstract (52 participant pairs), Section 1, Section 4.2 and the conclusion repeat 52 dyads.
confirmed.locator: p. 6, Section 4.3; p. 1, Abstract and Section 1; p. 4, Section 4.2; p. 14, Section 8

confirmed.statement: Every phase shows the same arm sizes. Figure 1 prints 26 vs 26 dyads for the main test and the immediate post-test and 52 vs 52 people for the retention post-test. The legends of Figures 4 to 12 read nAI = 26 dyads, nCONTROL = 26 dyads.

The counts are people. Five of the six sample shares fit 104 exactly: male 81/104 = 77.88%, female 23/104 = 22.12%, talked regularly 61/104 = 58.65%, prior generative AI use 103/104 = 99.04%, a few times a month to a few times a week 80/104 = 76.92% (my arithmetic). The sixth, 71.43% who knew their partner, fits no k/104 (74/104 = 71.15%) but fits 70/98, so that item likely had missing answers or a typo. It is a descriptive item and touches no outcome count.

The AI arm has 52 people. Figure 13 reads 'means, nAI = 52', and the Section 5.2 shares fit 52 exactly: 50/52 = 96.15%, 42/52 = 80.77%, 4/52 = 7.69% (twice), 2/52 = 3.85% (sum 52); 9/52 = 17.31%, 29/52 = 55.77%, 14/52 = 26.92% (sum 52) (my arithmetic).

The balance tests compare people, 52 vs 52. Age U = 1038.5 and private AI use U = 1631.0 both exceed 676, the largest U possible for 26 vs 26. Under 52 vs 52 the untied normal p is 0.0415 for age (printed 0.038) and 0.0697 for AI use (printed 0.040, which needs a large tie correction, possible for an ordinal frequency item). The elaboration U values (924.0, 970.0) give p = 0.0054 and 0.0130 under 52 vs 52 (printed 0.005 and 0.012), as the form's open_questions[0] says (my arithmetic).
confirmed.locator: p. 6, Section 4.3; p. 8, Section 5.1.1; p. 9, Section 5.1.2

confirmed.statement: n_randomized = null for S1 and both arms is right. Dyads were randomly assigned on arrival, participation was offered in English and in German, only native or advanced German-speaking dyads were kept 'for the final sample', and no page gives the number of dyads booked, tested, randomized, or dropped. Footnote 3 gives only the planned minimum of 20 dyads per condition. Any dyad tested and then dropped under the language rule was dropped after assignment.
confirmed.locator: p. 5, Sections 4.2.1-4.2.2; p. 6, Section 4.3 and footnote 3

confirmed.statement: No AI dyad drops out within the on-site session. Section 5.3 counts 16 of the 26 dyads at the first item and 15 out of 26 at the third. Table 3 lists 26, 26 and 25 first prompts, so one AI dyad sent ChatGPT-4 no prompt on the third object but is still counted at that item.

Retention attrition is not reported. The text never says how many people did the online retention post-test. Figure 1 shows 52 vs 52, and the Figure 12 legend reads 26 vs 26 dyads, as the form's exclusions field says. The final questionnaire on interim AI use has no reported results.
confirmed.locator: p. 5, Figure 1; p. 6, Section 4.2.4; p. 9, Section 5.1.3; p. 10, Figure 12

confirmed.statement: The who, population and country fields fit the text: Computer Science students from a 2nd-semester introductory lecture on data science and AI at 'an Austrian university', aged 18 to 35 (mean 21.55), 77.88% male, 99.04% prior generative AI use, a 5% course-grade bonus, and slots booked by two people so friends could pair up. Ethics approval came from 'our university, Graz University of Technology', and testing was on campus. The TU Graz site is an inference from those sentences, not a direct statement.
confirmed.locator: p. 5, Sections 4.2.1-4.2.2; p. 6, Section 4.3; p. 14, Section 7

confirmed.statement: participants.quote is verbatim (the PDF adds footnote marker 3), and participants.locator points to the right sections and figure.
confirmed.locator: p. 6, Section 4.3; p. 5, Section 4.2.1 and Figure 1

confirmed.statement: S1 and S2 share no people. S2's 20 dyads came from the face-to-face group of an Oct-Nov 2023 study of mostly psychology students who did not know each other, and c032 says the pre-study came before this study and fed its hypotheses. S1 tested Computer Science students on campus from March 11 to 23, 2024. The S2 people also appear in c151 and in that earlier study, and the form's sample_overlap names [7].
confirmed.locator: c032 p. 4, Sections 3 and 4.1; p. 5, Figure 1 and Section 4.2.2; [7] p. 3, Sections 4.2-4.3

confirmed.statement: S2's printed tests fit 10 chatbots vs 20 dyads, the team unit the form uses: U = 25.0 gives p = 0.0010 and U = 147.0 gives p = 0.039 (printed 0.001 and 0.041). With 10 vs 40 people they would give p below 0.0001 and p = 0.20 (my arithmetic). [7] labels its figures n_dyads = 20, n_AI = 10.

No other paper on file reuses the S1 sample. Atzori et al. (2026), Disley et al. (2026) and Lin et al. (2026) cite Bangerl et al. as literature only. Candidates c065 (Hemmatian et al. 2026, search record N = 62) and c581 (Tang et al. 2025, N = 202) are AUT dyad studies by other teams. A web search found no second report of the March 2024 experiment.

Criterion 2 holds on S1 alone: 104 people analyzed, 52 per arm. It would hold even if dyads were counted (52). The codebook's exclusion of pairs concerns pairs of outputs; these are pairs of people, and each person counts.

summary: The c032 PDF supports every S1 count in the form: 52 dyads (104 Computer Science students) were analyzed, 26 dyads and 52 people per arm in every phase, the number randomized before the German-language rule is never printed so n_randomized = null is right, no retention attrition is reported, and S1 alone clears 50 people. The coding is refuted only on details: S2 records 20 dyads as a team count although the paper defines a dyad as two humans and the pre-study paper [7] states 40 participants, and the form's note that the Figure 14 correlation is labeled 26 dyads leaves out that its p = 0.002 fits 52 duplicated participant rows, not 26.
